article.title: Brain health in children born extremely preterm: a multidimensional perspective
article.abstract: Gestational age and developmental stage of the brain at birth are major determinants of child health, and long-term consequences of preterm birth and altered brain maturation are inadequately understood simply through brain injury, survival rates, or diagnostic labels. In this Review, we conceptualise brain health in children born extremely preterm (before 28 weeks' gestation) as a developmental condition shaped by maturational timing, biological vulnerability, neonatal intensive care exposure, sensory and relational experiences, family circumstances, and social environments. We integrate evidence from research on early brain development and consciousness, long-term multidomain neurodevelopmental outcomes, neonatal intensive care practice, relational caregiving, early developmental interventions, and ethical, psychological, and social dimensions of care. Across these domains, extremely preterm birth emerges not as a single event but as a neuroplastic system that adapts to biological and environmental risks and protective factors that shape neurodevelopmental resilience and vulnerabilities and establish developmental trajectories. We argue that care for the infant born extremely preterm is optimised through a brain-health framework where care becomes a longitudinal, ethical process that integrates family support, minimises harmful exposures, promotes adaptive development, and fosters participation, wellbeing, and quality of life.

article.title: Satisfaction, Regret, and Harm After Hormone Therapy in Youth From a Multidisciplinary Gender Clinic
article.abstract:
Key Points Question What degrees of satisfaction, regret, and harm are reported by transgender and gender-diverse participants who initiated testosterone or estrogen therapy (ie, hormone therapy [HT]) as youth, and are these experiences associated with demographic or clinical characteristics? Findings In this cohort study of 372 participants who received care at a single multidisciplinary clinic, satisfaction with HT was high and regret and harm were rare. Decisional regret was slightly higher among youths not currently receiving HT and those identifying on the nonbinary spectrum, but it remained low in absolute terms. Meaning Results provide support for existing standards of care rather than broad restrictions on youths’ access to HT.

Importance Concerns about regret and harm have led to restrictions on transgender and gender-diverse youths’ access to testosterone or estrogen therapy (ie, hormone therapy [HT]), while empirical data on decisional regret among those initiating HT as youth remain limited. Objectives To examine satisfaction, regret, and perceived harm among individuals who initiated HT as youth and to identify demographic and clinical characteristics associated with regret or harm and current HT status (receiving vs not). Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study evaluates self-report surveys collected from October 2023 to October 2025 among former patients who initiated HT as youth at a single multidisciplinary gender clinic in the US. Data analysis was conducted from December 2025 to August 2026. Exposure Initiation of estrogen or testosterone. Main Outcomes and Measures Decision Regret Scale (DRS) total score (range, 0-100; higher scores indicate greater regret); item-level satisfaction, regret, and perceived harm; and current HT status. Associations with demographic and clinical characteristics were examined using nonparametric, Welch t , Fisher exact, or Pearson χ 2 tests as appropriate, with parametric sensitivity analyses for the DRS total score. Results Of the 376 participants who initiated HT as youth (112 [29.8%] initiating estrogen and 264 [70.2%] initiating testosterone; current age, 14-28 years; mean [SD] age, 20.9 [2.9] years; time since HT initiation: range, 1.2 months to 10.7 years; mean [SD], 4.9 [2.5] years), 4 were missing DRS scores, all of whom were currently receiving HT. Among the 372 respondents with DRS scores, overall decisional regret was very low (mean [SD] DRS score, 4.3 [14.7]; median [IQR], 0 [0-0]); 360 participants (96.8%) endorsed that receiving HT was the right decision, 10 (2.7%) reported regret, and 7 (1.9%) reported perceived harm. DRS scores were higher among participants not currently receiving HT vs currently receiving HT and among those identifying on the nonbinary vs binary spectrum; parametric sensitivity analyses estimated mean differences of 15.95 points (95% CI, 8.50-23.39) and 6.07 points (95% CI, 2.15-9.99), respectively. Participants not currently receiving HT (65 participants [17.3%]) were more likely than those currently receiving HT (311 [82.7%]) to have received testosterone (odds ratio, 3.58; 95% CI, 1.65-7.78; P = .001) and identify on the nonbinary spectrum (odds ratio, 8.88; 95% CI, 4.76-16.58; P < .001), were older (mean difference, 1.04 years; 95% CI, 0.45-1.64 years; P = .001), and had longer time since initiating HT (mean difference, 1.00 year; 95% CI, 0.48-1.53 years; P < .001). Neither regret or harm nor current HT status was associated with age at HT initiation or prepubertal gender diversity. Conclusions and Relevance The findings of this cohort study complement the literature documenting mental health benefits of HT, providing further support for existing standards of care for transgender and gender-diverse youth.

This cohort study examines satisfaction, regret, and perceived harm among individuals who initiated hormone therapy as youth and identifies demographic and clinical characteristics associated with regret or harm and current hormone therapy status.

Introduction Current estimates suggest that approximately 3.3% of 13- to 17-year-olds in the US identify as transgender or gender diverse (TGD). However, only a small proportion receive hormone therapy (HT; ie, testosterone, estrogen), with insurance-based analyses indicating rates below 0.1% of the general youth population. More than a dozen short-term follow-up studies and several large cross-sectional and retrospective studies have consistently found improvements in mental health and quality of life among TGD youth receiving HT. Prior research from our clinic found significant reductions in body dissatisfaction, depression, and anxiety and improvement in psychosocial functioning in 2 cohorts of youth 1 year after initiating HT and/or puberty suppression. This previous research indirectly suggests that TGD youth may be satisfied with HT. However, concerns about potential regret and harm have intensified, leading to widespread efforts to prevent minors from accessing HT despite standards of care continuing to support its use. While more limited in scope, several initial studies have demonstrated very low levels of regret among youth, consistent with low regret levels documented among TGD adults. One of the first major longitudinal studies of youth receiving HT reported that no participants expressed regret regarding puberty suppression or HT an average of 6 years after starting treatment. Three other clinic-based studies of youth have documented regret rates between 0% and 2%. These findings are also consistent with a community-based sample of youth who socially transitioned in childhood and later accessed HT. While the rate of regret was slightly higher in this sample (5 of 119 respondents [4.2%]), nearly all respondents (115 of 119 [96.6%]) reported satisfaction with treatment. Preliminary research also suggests that rates of treatment discontinuation are low for those initiating HT as youth. van der Loos et al reported that only 16 of 720 participants (2.2%) who started puberty suppression as adolescents were no longer receiving HT at median (IQR) follow-up of 3.5 (1.5-6.6) years later for youth assigned female and 2.3 (1.2-4.8) years later for youth assigned male. In another clinic-based sample with median follow-up of 2.7 years, 57 of 1050 participants (5.4%) initiating HT as youth discontinued HT for at least 3 months, although 20 subsequently restarted and 210 were lost to follow-up. In a third sample using a US military insurance database, the 4-year continuation rate for those starting HT as minors was somewhat lower (74%), but it was still higher than for those who started HT as adults (64%). Most studies examining reasons for stopping treatment have been conducted with adults, and findings suggest that stopping treatment is influenced by a range of internal and external factors and thus is not synonymous with regret. Given recent increases in external barriers to accessing HT, rates of stopping treatment are likely increasing. The present study seeks to strengthen the research base regarding TGD youths’ experiences with HT, considering the substantial shifts in access to HT and concerns about the well-being of youth receiving this care. Building on our previous work, our first aim was to examine the degree of perceived satisfaction, regret, and harm among youth who initiated HT, including those who were currently receiving HT as well as those who were not. Our second aim was to examine whether demographic and clinical factors were associated with (1) youths’ reports of regret or harm and/or (2) current HT status (receiving vs not). Methods Participants and Procedure Participants in this cohort study included former patients who were seen by a US multidisciplinary program for TGD youth and received HT. The process for initiating HT was guided by the World Professional Association for Transgender Health’s standards of care, version 7 (the current version at the time), and the Endocrine Society’s guidelines, which included a semistructured assessment with patients and their parent(s) or guardian(s) conducted by a mental health professional in the program. This assessment visit was designed specifically for patients potentially interested in initiating medical treatment. For patients younger than 18 years, consent for HT was required from all parent(s) or guardian(s) with legal medical decision-making rights in addition to patient assent. Regardless of whether they subsequently initiated medical treatment, patients and parents who participated in the assessment were also approached to provide assent or consent for the clinical information from their medical record to be used for research purposes as part of a study approved by the institutional review board at University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center. Consent from a parent or guardian was required for research participants who were minors (aged <18 years) at the time of assent. Starting October 2023, patients and parents who provided initial assent or consent were reapproached to complete a yearly online research survey as part of a newly funded National Institutes of Health study. Participants could complete the survey from 1 month before to 6 months after the yearly anniversary of their initial assessment. The present study uses data collected from October 2023 to October 2025. Recruitment materials encouraged former patients to participate even if they never started treatment, stopped treatment, and/or were no longer receiving care. While all participants completed an assessment with the program, a minority started HT before or after being seen by the program (eg, transferred care after moving). Participants were compensated $45 to $65; changes in compensation aligned with adding new measures. We followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology ( STROBE ) reporting guidelines. Data analysis was conducted from December 2025 to August 2026. Measures For treatments started prior to the participants’ last visit with the program, start dates documented in medical records were used. Self-report was used for any additional start and stop dates and participants’ current gender and sexual orientation identities. Participants’ assigned sex, race, and ethnicity were obtained from medical records when self-report was not available. Prepubertal onset of gender diversity was assessed by 3 yes vs no items completed by the clinician indicating the presence of gender nonconformity, physical dysphoria, and/or a stated gender identity different than assigned sex prior to puberty onset. Patients’ self-reported age at which they first identified with the gender identity reported at the initial assessment (hereafter termed age at first identification ) was also obtained from the assessment note. Participants completed the Decision Regret Scale (DRS), a 5-item measure with 5 response options prompting respondents to “reflect on your decision to start estrogen/testosterone therapy.” Total scores range from 0 to 100; higher scores indicate higher levels of decisional regret. For participants with multiple versions of the survey, the most recent version was used. However, all participants who agreed or strongly agreed that they experienced regret or harm on any version of the survey were included in analyses examining the subgroup of participants who reported regret or harm. Starting in October 2024, if a participant reported that they agreed or strongly agreed that they experienced regret or harm, they were prompted to describe their experiences in an open-ended text box. Statistical Analysis To characterize the sample, we compared patients who consented vs those who were not reached or who declined participation by age at initial assessment and assigned sex and ethnicity (Hispanic or Latino vs not Hispanic or Latino). Among those who consented, we also tested for differences between those who completed vs did not complete the survey by the same characteristics, prepubertal onset of gender diversity, and age at first identification. To characterize each participant’s perception of satisfaction, regret, and harm, we examined total scores on the DRS and responses on individual items reflecting the participant’s perceptions of whether they made the right decision, experienced regret, and were harmed by the treatment. We also examined whether assigned sex, current gender identity (dichotomized into binary vs nonbinary spectrum, excluding cisgender), prepubertal onset of gender diversity, age at first identification, age at HT initiation, current age, and time since initiating HT were associated with (1) DRS scores, (2) whether participants ever reported regret or harm, and (3) HT status (receiving vs not). Qualitative responses were grouped into themes based on consensus between coauthors. Given DRS scores showed substantial positive skew (4.7), kurtosis (23.9), and a pronounced floor effect (median [IQR], 0 [0-0]), nonparametric analyses were selected as a conservative primary approach. Spearman rank-order correlations examined associations between DRS scores and continuous variables, and Mann-Whitney U tests compared DRS score distributions across dichotomized variables, with effect sizes ( r ) computed from the standardized test statistic. Parametric analyses using Pearson correlations and Welch t test were also conducted as sensitivity analyses. Demographic and clinical characteristics were compared by regret or harm and current HT status using Welch t tests or Mann-Whitney U tests for markedly nonnormal continuous variables and Fisher exact or Pearson χ 2 tests for categorical variables, as appropriate. Effect estimates and 95% CIs were reported when applicable. Results Participants who consented to the initial study did not differ in age at initial assessment, assigned sex, or ethnicity from those who did not (eg, declined, not reached). However, among those who initially consented, those assigned male and those who experienced physical dysphoria prior to puberty were less likely to complete the current survey. No other differences were found between these groups. Figure 1 provides a flowchart of participant inclusion. Table 1 and Table 2 provide information on participant demographic and clinical characteristics separated by current HT status and ever experiencing regret or harm from receiving HT. Within the study sample of 376 participants who initiated HT as youth (112 [29.8%] initiating estrogen and 264 [70.2%] initiating testosterone), participants’ current age ranged from 14 to 28 years (mean [SD] age, 20.9 [2.9] years); 344 participants (91.7%) started HT at age 17 years or younger, 27 (7.2%) at age 18 years, and 4 (1.1%) at age 19 years. Time since initiating HT ranged from 1.2 months to 10.7 years (mean [SD], 4.9 [2.5] years); 311 participants (82.7%) were receiving HT at the time of the survey and 65 participants (17.3%) were not. article.title: Theoretical frameworks of extended reality interventions for eating and weight disorders and beyond: A systematic umbrella review
article.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Extended reality (XR) is increasingly used in mental health treatment, including eating and weight disorders (EWD), due to its potential to target disorder-relevant mechanisms in immersive environments. This umbrella review synthesizes theoretical frameworks guiding XR-based psychotherapeutic applications. Our findings have also implications for other mental health disorders as they provide a framework on transdiagnostic mechanisms of XR-based interventions.

METHODS: Systematic searches of PubMed, PsycINFO, and Cochrane identified 44 review articles on XR-based psychotherapeutic interventions in EWD, including systematic and non-systematic reviews. Methodological quality was assessed using AMSTAR 2 and SANRA. The umbrella review was conducted and reported in accordance with PRISMA 20 guidelines.

RESULTS: The majority of reviews (n = 37) reported underlying theoretical frameworks with varying depth and quality. Our synthesis organizes these into a two-level taxonomy comprising first-order therapeutic mechanisms (behavioral, intersectional, and cognitive) and second-order XR-specific modulators (presence, embodiment, and the Proteus Effect).

CONCLUSIONS: XR appears to enhance established psychological mechanisms rather than generate novel therapeutic processes. A mechanism-oriented framework separating therapeutic mechanisms from XR-specific modulators may guide the development of more targeted and clinically precise XR interventions. Further experimental research is needed to validate mechanisms of action and optimize XR applications in EWD and beyond.
